answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: Consequential accounting methods, by their focus on measuring future changes in emissions due to an action undertaken rather than measuring present emissions, can further incentivize emissions-reducing actions and projects. The biggest challenges with the development and use of consequential accounting methods involve verification of projected changes in future emissions and the associated cost of verification, as well as reconciling emissions calculated under attributional accounting for a present time period with what emissions for that same time period were projected to be under consequential accounting, whenever the emissions figures from both these methods differ.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: The two formula factors of electricity consumption per transaction/hour and the marginal emission rate per unit of electricity for a given region/time/conditions are appropriately indicative for the formula to quantify effectively the emissions impact of electricity projects.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: Secondary effects that should be considered are emissions changes in fuel extraction, refining and transportation, as well as in fugitive and vented emissions and from biofuel consumption. These emissions changes can be quantified using the emissions rates and projected changes in consumption of the fuels involved compared to the baseline scenario.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Reporting the emissions impacts of electricity projects every year, instead of once as a lifetime total, more effectively enables verification that emissions impacts of electricity projects are occurring as projected throughout the lifetime of the project.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: For regulatory and timing tests, both are already utilized in multiple other additionality frameworks, indicating widespread recognition of their principles as a useful basis for demonstrating additionality. For common practice tests, it is fair to consider widely implemented types of projects as mainstream, and avoided emissions should not be due to actions that everyone else in a region/sector is also doing. For positive lists, green and net zero technologies contributing to reductions in emissions, which also tend to be newer, less adopted technologies, are a useful basis for demonstrating additionality. But the concern that a positive list can be too broad and end up misused is significant enough that a positive list should only be optional. For performance standard tests, a quantitative benchmark in baseline emissions rate, renewable penetration level, etc. is also a useful basis for demonstrating additionality, but other tests are more useful, hence why a performance standard test should only be optional. For first-of-its-kind tests, the introduction of a new technology, scale or application to a market/region, by its very nature, is different from mainstream practices in that market/region, and on that basis should be considered a useful test of additionality.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: Only the contractual/tenor test may not be feasible as a test of additionality, as the financing for a project may have been provided and/or construction started before a long-term contract or commitment with a buyer has been secured. The other eight additionality tests listed in question 28 are all feasible. The regulatory test is feasible as it is simply requires referring to existing laws and regulations and verifying whether the activity is already required under those laws and regulations. The timing test, financial analysis test, barrier test and performance standard test are all feasible using project documentation from the early stages of the project process, where any incentives that were decisive to barriers overcome, expected financial returns, and/or projected outperformances of key benchmarks, as well as to the project going ahead, would be recorded. The common practice test and first-of-its-kind test are both feasible by comparing a project and its technologies/scale/applications used with other projects in the same market/region. The positive list is feasible as project details can be cross-referenced with the list of technologies, project types and/or circumstances that automatically demonstrate additionality.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: There are no other additionality tests outside the nine listed in question 28 that should be included in an additionality framework. I instead suggest the inclusion of a requirement that the baseline emissions scenario used for any additionality test for a project be updated on a 2 to 5 year basis, in order to more accurately measure avoided emissions.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text: The most appropriate methodologies for determining operating margin emission rates for renewable energy projects are the ones that can use empirical or recorded data to quantify emission rates, which is the case for both SCED sensitivity analysis, statistical, and capacity factor based methodologies. In contrast, scenario modeling, heat-rate/LMP, and difference-based approaches all use estimates rather than hard data to quantify operating margin emission rates, and while using estimates can still yield accurate emission rates, it will not be as accurate as emission rates quantified based on hard data.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text: The recent capacity addition methodology is the only one of the four build margin methodologies to use empirical data in its calculations, and on that basis should be considered appropriate for quantifying build margin emission rates for renewable energy projects. The policy scenario methodology, due to its basis in countries' existing and planned national energy policies as summed up in the Stated Policies Scenario, should also be considered appropriate. The capacity expansion modeling methodology, through its simulations of multiple grid capacity change scenarios, can also be appropriate for quantifying build margin emission rates. Only the average emission factor methodology would not be appropriate, as averaging existing grid generation is a more generalized and less accurate methodology for quantifying build margin emission rates compared to the other methodologies that use hard, specific data or detailed existing and planned national policies.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: One significant factor, through which GHG Protocol can assess the applicability of emission rate methodologies towards different types of projects, is project scope. Operating margin emission rates may be more appropriate for projects that only significantly impact the marginal generators in a grid, or whose impact on the grid can be described as a one-time change. Build margin emission rates, on the other hand, may be better suited to larger scope projects that significantly impact the entire grid or whose impact on the grid occurs over multiple phases in time.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text: Some of the operating margin and build margin emission rates methodologies can also be adapted for use in projects covering ground, marine and air transport, with each vehicle being treated like a marginal unit and an entire vehicle fleet as the equivalent of a power grid for the purposes of measuring emissions impacts.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: Grid region was selected as it is the next most granular spatial boundary after the country level, which a majority of the global coverage OMER datasets listed in section 8.1 function at. Setting the maximum appropriate spatial granularity level at grid region creates an impetus for these global OMER datasets to transition to this more granular spatial boundary, improving the detail, quality and applicability of global OMER data for all users. In addition to this, GHG Protocol should also take a proactive role in initiating a transition by all OMER datasets towards a nodal level of spatial granularity in the long-term.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: There is already a push towards the use of hourly data in the proposed revision to the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Emissions Standard. Having the maximum appropriate level of temporal granularity for OMER and BMER data be broader than the hourly level will hinder the transition to hourly data that is being pushed for in other emissions standards.

answers.label: Appropriate margin weighting approaches
selections: GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text: GHG Protocol's own Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Emissions from Grid-Connected Electricity Projects, by its nature of being a complementary tool in GHG Protocol's full slate of standards and other resources, should be considered appropriate for assigning build and operating margin weights to electricity projects. CDM Tool07 is developed by the world's most significant climate change authority in the UNFCCC, whose credibility makes CDM Tool07 appropriate for assigning build and operating margin weights. In addition to these two, intervention lifecycle approaches are an appropriate tool, as whether or not a project is already anticipated in capacity planning, and by extension already part of a large-scale change to the grid, is a useful indicator to determine the extent to apply operating and/or build margin rates to the project.
